reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive defect of bile acid synthesis caused by deficiency of the mitochondrial enzyme sterol 27-hydroxylase (CYP27A1)
The block impairs bile acid production and diverts cholesterol to cholestanol, which accumulates in the brain, tendons and other tissues
A highly treatable but frequently missed cause of progressive neurological decline; early diagnosis is critical to prevent irreversible damage
The classic triad comprises tendon xanthomata (especially the Achilles tendon), early-onset (juvenile) bilateral cataracts and progressive neuropsychiatric and cerebellar dysfunction
Early clues in childhood include neonatal cholestasis, intractable or chronic diarrhoea and learning difficulty, preceding the neurological syndrome
The biochemical hallmark is raised plasma cholestanol with normal or low cholesterol and increased urinary bile alcohols
Treatment is replacement with chenodeoxycholic acid, which suppresses abnormal synthesis and can halt or improve disease if started early; a statin may be added
reference.pathophysiology: Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis is caused by deficiency of sterol 27-hydroxylase, an enzyme in the mitochondrial pathway of bile acid synthesis from cholesterol. Loss of this step reduces production of the primary bile acid chenodeoxycholic acid, removing the normal negative feedback on the rate-limiting enzyme of bile acid synthesis and driving overproduction of bile acid intermediates. These intermediates are shunted into cholestanol and bile alcohols, which accumulate in tissues. Deposition of cholestanol and cholesterol in the central nervous system, tendons and lens produces the characteristic xanthomata, cataracts and progressive neurodegeneration. Replacing the deficient bile acid restores feedback inhibition and reduces the toxic accumulation.
additionalDifferentials: Other hereditary spastic paraplegias and cerebellar ataxias
Multiple sclerosis or other progressive neuroinflammatory disease
Early-onset dementia or leukodystrophy of other cause
Neonatal cholestasis from other bile acid synthesis defects
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing of the CYP27A1 gene
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain, which may show cerebellar and dentate nucleus changes
Slit-lamp examination for juvenile cataract and clinical assessment of tendon xanthomata
Lipid profile, noting cholesterol may be normal or low despite xanthomata
redFlags: Progressive cognitive, psychiatric or cerebellar decline in a young person with tendon xanthomata
Early-onset bilateral cataracts in a child or young adult
Neonatal cholestasis or intractable childhood diarrhoea of unknown cause
Delay in starting bile acid replacement, risking irreversible neurological damage
reference.prognosis: If chenodeoxycholic acid replacement is started before significant neurological damage, progression can be halted and some deficits improve, giving a good outlook; late diagnosis after established neurodegeneration carries a poorer prognosis with irreversible disability.
pitfalls: Assuming tendon xanthomata always indicate familial hypercholesterolaemia, since cholesterol is often normal here
Missing the diagnosis during the early non-neurological phase (cholestasis, diarrhoea, cataract)
Overlooking juvenile cataract as an early diagnostic clue
Delaying treatment while awaiting genetic confirmation, forfeiting a treatable window
Failing to screen and counsel at-risk relatives given the recessive inheritance
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
